note: Anaesthetised-rat drug-induced ejaculation models (7-OH-DPAT or apomorphine; seminal-vesicle pressure + bulbospongiosus EMG) predicted that blocking central oxytocin receptors delays ejaculation; epelsiban failed Phase 2 (2013) and brain-penetrant cligosiban split its two Phase 2 trials (2019).
label: Premature ejaculation (OXTR)

engagement.model: Anaesthetised rat, 7-OH-DPAT-induced ejaculation, antagonist by i.v. vs i.c.v. vs intrathecal route
engagement.note: A peptide OT antagonist blocked drug-induced ejaculation only when given into the brain or L6 cord, defining a central target.
engagement.short: Rat: target is brain OT receptor
engagement.quote: Brain oxytocin receptors mediate male sexual responses elicited by i.c.v. 7-OH-DPAT in anaesthetized rats whereas L6 spinal oxytocin receptors only impair the occurrence of ejaculation.

engagement.model: Rat CSF:plasma after IV infusion plus OT-mediated NTS neuronal firing (anaesthetised rat)
engagement.note: Rat showed good CNS penetration and central OT pharmacology; healthy men had CSF cligosiban at ~40% of unbound plasma.
engagement.quote: Cligosiban was detected in CSF at concentrations approximately 40% of unbound plasma concentrations.
engagement.reason: CSF penetration matched rat; no occupancy
engagement.judgement: Called `same` on CNS exposure, not receptor occupancy: the rat prediction (Wayman 2018, doi 10.1016/j.jsxm.2018.10.008, 'After systemic dosing to rats, cligosiban showed good CNS penetration') was CNS penetration, and the human read-out is CSF drug in healthy volunteers, not a pharmacodynamic marker in patients. Both sources read at abstract level (J Sex Med paywalled); I juxtaposed them, the Osterloh paper does not cite the rat ratio. Downgrade to `untested` if CSF exposure is not accepted as engagement.

dose.model: Anaesthetised rat EMG ejaculation model (cligosiban 0.9 mg/kg IV bolus)
dose.note: Phase 1 doses were described as 'predicted to be therapeutic', but no rat exposure target was ever published against patient exposure.
dose.quote: Cligosiban had a good safety/tolerability profile at doses predicted to be therapeutic or supra-therapeutic and a pharmacokinetic profile appropriate for "as-needed" dosing for men with PE.
dose.reason: No exposure target published vs patients
dose.judgement: Wayman 2018 gives only a rat dose (0.9 mg/kg IV) in the abstract; whether the full text states a plasma/CSF target that PEPIX/PEDRIX (400-1200 mg) were designed to hit could not be checked (paywalled). No source compares rat effective exposure with patient exposure, so untested.

efficacy.model: Anaesthetised rat, 7-OH-DPAT-induced ejaculation (seminal-vesicle pressure + bulbospongiosus EMG)
efficacy.note: A central OT antagonist blocked drug-induced ejaculation in anaesthetised rats; the authors proposed the model for PE drug development.
efficacy.short: Rat ejaculation model proposed for PE
efficacy.quote: These findings should be considered for the development of potential pharmacological treatment of premature ejaculation in man.

efficacy.model: Anaesthetised rat, 7-OH-DPAT-induced ejaculation (epelsiban/GSK557296 i.v., i.c.v., intrathecal)
efficacy.note: Epelsiban inhibited rat ejaculation (best when given centrally); 50 or 150 mg before sex did not change IELT vs placebo in 77 men.
efficacy.short: Epelsiban: rat delay, no IELT gain
efficacy.quote: Epelsiban 50 mg and 150 mg were well tolerated, but did not result in a clinically or statistically significant change in IELT in men with PE, compared with placebo.
efficacy.judgement: Model side is Clement 2013 (doi 10.1111/bph.12198, Br J Pharmacol 169:1477): 'Targeting central OT receptors with highly selective antagonist seems a promising approach for the treatment of premature ejaculation.' I juxtaposed the two papers; the Shinghal discussion is paywalled so I could not confirm it cites the rat data. Caveat: in the rat, systemic (i.v.) GSK557296 worked only at the highest dose and left the BS-EMG untouched, with central delivery most effective, so an alternative reading is an engagement failure (poor CNS penetration) rather than a model failure; no source states epelsiban's human CNS penetration, so I did not use that to rescue the model.

efficacy.model: Anaesthetised rat, apomorphine-induced ejaculation (bulbospongiosus EMG), cligosiban 0.9 mg/kg IV
efficacy.note: Brain-penetrant cligosiban inhibited rat ejaculation; PEPIX (n=88) raised IELT 1.9-fold vs placebo, but PEDRIX (n=239) found no difference at 400-1200 mg.
efficacy.quote: There were no clinically or statistically significant differences between cligosiban (at any dose level) and placebo for the primary endpoint (change in geometric IELT) or any of the secondary endpoints.
efficacy.reason: Larger trial negative; rat prediction failed
efficacy.judgement: Same-status entry added deliberately: the 2013 miss could be blamed on epelsiban's engagement, whereas cligosiban removed that excuse ('first highly selective and centrally penetrant OT receptor antagonist', Wayman 2018) and the model still missed in the adequately powered trial. PEPIX (McMahon 2019, doi 10.1016/j.jsxm.2019.05.016, NCT02232425, results posted 2019-01-24): fold-change ratio 1.9, P = .0079; PEDRIX (NCT03055806, results posted 2019-10-07): negative, 'The reasons for this disparity are not known.' No primary source attributes the reversal to the rat model, rat-vs-human receptor pharmacology, or CNS penetration; the only published explanation is placebo response, in letters (Pyke 2019, doi 10.1016/j.jsxm.2019.08.010: 33% vs 20% placebo allocation; authors' reply doi 10.1016/j.jsxm.2019.08.023: 'In the unsuccessful trial, the placebo response was greater (43.1-second or 1.8-fold)'). Wayman 2018 itself cautioned: 'The translation of the animal models of ejaculation to PE in man is unproven.' Stadler 2021 (FASEB J, doi 10.1096/fj.202100435R) merely notes the split as 'Surprisingly'. Rule 5 applied: contra from the 2019 PEDRIX publication, not from later knowledge. All J Sex Med texts read at abstract level (paywalled).
